title: What is the difference between the eager and cooperative-sticky rebalance protocols?
keyPoints: Eager rebalance is stop-the-world: every consumer revokes all partitions and the whole group pauses during reassignment.
Cooperative-sticky rebalance is incremental: consumers keep their current partitions and only migrating partitions pause.
Eager uses RangeAssignor or RoundRobinAssignor; cooperative uses CooperativeStickyAssignor.
Cooperative-sticky dramatically reduces the impact of rolling deployments because most consumers never stop processing.
Migration from eager to cooperative requires a two-phase rolling upgrade to avoid protocol conflicts.
Static group membership (group.instance.id) complements cooperative rebalancing by avoiding rebalance on quick restarts.
Commit offsets in onPartitionsRevoked so no work is double-processed after a rebalance.

s1_definition.oneliner: Eager revokes all partitions and pauses the whole group; cooperative-sticky keeps existing assignments and only moves the partitions that truly need to move.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Eager protocol** -- a stop-the-world rebalance where every consumer revokes all its partitions, the group recomputes assignments from scratch, and all consumers pause during the shuffle.
- **Cooperative-sticky protocol** -- an incremental rebalance where consumers keep partitions they already own and only the specific partitions that must move are revoked, usually over two short rebalances.
- **RangeAssignor / RoundRobinAssignor** -- built-in assignors that use the eager protocol.
- **CooperativeStickyAssignor** -- the built-in assignor that uses the cooperative-sticky protocol.
- **Static group membership** -- setting `group.instance.id` so a briefly restarting consumer rejoins without triggering any rebalance within the session timeout.
- **onPartitionsRevoked** -- a callback where you commit offsets before partitions are taken away to prevent double-processing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India reassigning counters among tellers when a new teller joins. Eager rebalancing is like telling every teller to leave their counter and stand in the hallway, then handing out counter assignments again from scratch -- the whole bank stops serving customers during the reshuffle. Cooperative-sticky rebalancing is like saying most of you keep your current counters; only two counters need to move to the new teller. Almost everyone keeps serving customers and only the few affected counters pause briefly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The eager and cooperative-sticky protocols are two ways a consumer group redistributes partitions when membership changes. The eager protocol is stop-the-world: every consumer revokes all partitions, the group recomputes a fresh assignment, and then everyone picks up their new partitions. Even consumers whose partitions do not change still give them up and take them back, so the entire group pauses for the duration.

The cooperative-sticky protocol is incremental. Consumers keep the partitions they already own, and only the specific partitions that need to move are revoked over two short rebalances. At National Bank of India, Pankaj moved the settlement consumers from eager to cooperative-sticky because every rolling deploy produced visible latency spikes from the whole group stopping. Now a deploy only pauses the partitions owned by the restarting consumer.

Static group membership with `group.instance.id` complements cooperative rebalancing by letting a quickly restarting consumer rejoin without triggering any rebalance at all. The migration from eager to cooperative requires a two-phase rolling upgrade because the assignors disagree on revocation semantics.

Remember one sentence: cooperative-sticky turns a routine consumer restart from a group-wide outage into a localized, barely noticeable event.
